title: Question 8
stem: A polished sheet of magnesium in a vacuum emits electrons when it is illuminated by ultraviolet radiation.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State the name of this phenomenon.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what is happening here - light is hitting a metal surface in a vacuum and electrons are escaping from the surface. What is the standard name for light-induced electron emission?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise Light Ejecting Electrons**
You have ultraviolet radiation falling on magnesium and electrons coming straight out of the metal. This one-to-one interaction where a photon gives its energy to a surface electron to release it is called the photoelectric effect.

enrichment.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what is happening here - light is hitting a metal surface in a vacuum and electrons are escaping from the surface. What is the standard name for light-induced electron emission?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise Light Ejecting Electrons**

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: For emission of electrons to occur, the frequency of the ultraviolet radiation must be at least $8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{Hz}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the work function energy of magnesium.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the meaning of the minimum frequency $8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$. At this threshold frequency the emitted electrons just escape with zero kinetic energy, so all the photon energy goes into freeing the electron.
Hint 2: Use the photon energy relation with Planck constant $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and the threshold frequency $f_0$ to find the work function $\Phi$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Threshold Frequency to Work Function**
At the threshold frequency $f_0$, the photon just has enough energy to free the electron. There is no leftover kinetic energy. So the work function $\Phi$ equals the photon energy at threshold.

Step 2: **Calculate $\Phi = h f_0$**
$$\Phi = h f_0$$ $$\Phi = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (8.8 \times 10^{14})$$ $$\Phi = 5.8 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

enrichment.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the meaning of the minimum frequency $8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$. At this threshold frequency the emitted electrons just escape with zero kinetic energy, so all the photon energy goes into freeing the electron.
Hint 2: Use the photon energy relation with Planck constant $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$ and the threshold frequency $f_0$ to find the work function $\Phi$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Threshold Frequency to Work Function**
At the threshold frequency $f_0$, the photon just has enough energy to free the electron. There is no leftover kinetic energy. So the work function $\Phi$ equals the photon energy at threshold.

Step 2: **Calculate $\Phi = h f_0$**
$$\Phi = h f_0$$ $$\Phi = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (8.8 \times 10^{14})$$ $$\Phi = 5.8 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: For ultraviolet radiation with a frequency of $11 \times 10^{14} \text{Hz}$, calculate the maximum speed of the emitted electrons.
hints: Hint 1: Think energy accounting - the incoming photon energy is now larger than the minimum needed to escape. Where does the extra energy go for the fastest electrons?
Hint 2: Write down Einstein's photoelectric equation linking photon energy to work function plus maximum kinetic energy, then substitute $E_{MAX} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{MAX}^2$.
Hint 3: Calculate the photon energy at $11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$, subtract your $\Phi$ from (b)(i) to get $E_{MAX}$, then rearrange for $v_{MAX}$ using $m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply Conservation of Energy**
Each photon is absorbed by one electron. Part of the energy does the work of escaping, the rest becomes kinetic energy. For the fastest electrons:
$$h f = \Phi + E_{MAX}$$ where $E_{MAX} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{MAX}^2$.

Step 2: **Find the Leftover Kinetic Energy**
Photon energy at $f = 11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$:
$$h f = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (11 \times 10^{14}) = 7.29 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$
Subtract the work function:
$$E_{MAX} = h f - \Phi = 7.29 \times 10^{-19} - 5.83 \times 10^{-19} \approx 1.46 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Convert Kinetic Energy to Speed**
$$\frac{1}{2} m v_{MAX}^2 = 1.46 \times 10^{-19}$$
$$v_{MAX} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.46 \times 10^{-19}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}}$$
$$v_{MAX} = 5.7 \times 10^5 \text{ m s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (c)

markscheme_points.text: EMAX shown as zero from f = 8.0 to 8.8 and non-zero from f = 8.8 to 11
all non-zero EMAX shown as a single straight line with a positive gradient

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens below the threshold frequency of $8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$. Are any electrons emitted, and what does that mean for $E_{MAX}$ on the graph?
Hint 2: Recall the form $E_{MAX} = h f - \Phi$. If you plot $E_{MAX}$ against $f$, what shape should the part above threshold have and what is its gradient?

Hint 3: Use your value from (b)(ii) to find the top point of the sketch: at $f = 11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$, $E_{MAX} \approx 1.45 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$. Where must the sloping line start on the f-axis?
parts.proper_answer: Sketch: $E_{MAX}=0$ from $8.0$ to $8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$, then a straight line of positive gradient from $(8.8, 0)$ to $(11, 1.45 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J})$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Show Zero Emission Below Threshold**
For $f < 8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ the photon energy $h f$ is less than $\Phi$, so no electrons escape. Draw $E_{MAX} = 0$ flat along the f-axis from $8.0$ to $8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$.

Step 2: **Draw the Straight Line Above Threshold**
From $E_{MAX} = h f - \Phi$, $E_{MAX}$ grows linearly with $f$ with gradient $h$. So from $f = 8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ upwards, draw a single straight line with positive gradient. It starts at zero at the threshold.

Step 3: **Fix the Top Point**
At $f = 11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ you already found $E_{MAX} \approx 1.46 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$. So the line must pass through:
$$f = 11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}, \quad E_{MAX} = 1.45 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$
Check the axes: vertical is $E_{MAX}/10^{-19} \text{ J}$ so this is 1.45 on that scale, horizontal is $f/10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ so this is 11.0.
